input.narrative:
The lantern's light steadies again, throwing a long amber wash across the wet stones, and you follow it toward the harbourmaster's shed, where a hunched figure sits mending a coil of rope with fingers thick as knots themselves.

She doesn't look up right away. When she does, her eyes are pale and tired, rimmed with the particular exhaustion of someone who has spent too many nights waiting on a wharf for something that isn't coming back.

"You're the mason," she says, not a question. "Built that wall out past the point. Good work. Held through the spring gales when half the old pier didn't." She sets the rope down, wipes her palms on her apron, and studies you properly now. "But you didn't climb down here in the dark to talk about stonework."

"I heard there's a ship missing," you say. "The *Wren's Daughter*, someone said at the tavern. Out three days past when she should've been back in one."

Her jaw tightens, just slightly, a small flinch quickly smoothed over. "Four days," she corrects. "Not three. I keep the log myself, mason, I don't need the tavern's arithmetic." She reaches for a ledger on the shelf behind her, opens it to a page marked with a strip of tar-blackened twine, and turns it so you can see the neat, cramped hand recording departures and returns. The entry for the *Wren's Daughter* has no return mark beside it. Just a gap, waiting.

"Storm took her, most like," she goes on, though there's something in the way she says it that doesn't sound convinced of her own words. "Though the weather's been fair enough this week to make a liar of that notion. Fair enough that three other boats came in without a scratch on them." She taps the empty space in the ledger with one blunt finger. "Her captain was Ossian. Careful man. Wouldn't have run her onto rocks he didn't know, and he knew every rock in this harbour like the back of his own hand."

*A careful man, in fair weather, four days gone.* You feel the unease settle into your chest the way damp settles into old mortar — slow, and impossible to shift once it's in.

"Any wreckage come ashore?" you ask. "Anything at all?"

The harbourmaster's mouth thins. She glances toward the shed door, toward the dark water beyond the lantern's reach, and lowers her voice as though the harbour itself might be listening. "One thing," she admits. "A length of her rigging, cut clean — not snapped, not frayed. *Cut.* Found it tangled round a mooring post out by the old breakwater two mornings ago, and I haven't told a soul but you, because the last thing this harbour needs is folk whispering about wreckers again." She fixes you with a look that is equal parts warning and appeal. "You build walls to keep the sea out, mason. Maybe you're the sort who notices what doesn't fit. I could use a pair of eyes I trust down at that breakwater, come first light. Or you could forget I said any of this and go back to your stones."

The lantern gutters once more between you, throwing her face half into shadow, half into gold, and she waits for your answer with the stillness of someone who has already guessed which one you'll give.

quick_actions.text: Ask her who else knows about the cut rigging before committing to anything
Tell her you'll go to the breakwater tonight, by lantern light
Ask to see the cut rigging for yourself right now

input.scene_description: Inside a weathered wooden harbourmaster shed at night, lit by a flickering brass lantern hanging from a beam. A stocky, weathered woman in her fifties with pale tired eyes and a tar-stained apron sits at a cluttered desk, a ledger open before her, a coil of rope in her lap. Across from her stands a rugged stonemason, broad-shouldered, dust and mortar still on his rough work clothes, listening intently. Through the open door, dark harbour water and moored boats are faintly visible under a starless sky.
